# Bej Off The Record

> Music history channel by Bej on TikTok, Instagram and YouTube. Short episodes with names, dates and an opinion: Mexican music history decade by decade, biographies of rock frontwomen, music video directors, and Cover Atlas, which follows one song through its versions in other countries and languages. Site in English, German and Spanish.

## Series
- [World Music History](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/world-music-history/): Mexican music history, decade by decade. From ranchera and bolero to rock, norteño, cumbia and Canto Nuevo.
- [Frontwoman](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/frontwoman/): The women who ran the stage, told as lives, not legends. Debbie Harry, Brody Dalle, Shirley Manson.
- [Video Essays](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/video-essays/): One artist, taken apart over several episodes. Technique, effect, and why.
- [Director Series](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/director-series/): The directors who decided what music looks like. Chris Cunningham, Diane Martel, Mary Lambert, Joseph Kahn, Dave Meyers and more.
- [Cover Atlas](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/cover-atlas/): One song, every language it travelled into.
- [Taking It Off The Shelf](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/taking-it-off-the-shelf/): One band, one song from every album. Under a minute.
- [On This Day in Music History](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/on-this-day/): Birthdays and moments that shaped music, one date at a time.
- [Strokes Week](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/strokes-week/): A week of Strokes trivia to celebrate seeing them live.
- [Concert Diaries](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/concert-diaries/): What the night was actually like. Written after, posted after.

## Cover Atlas episodes
- [Bang Bang (My Baby Shot Me Down): the versions around the world](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/cover-atlas/bang-bang/): Sonny Bono wrote "Bang Bang (My Baby Shot Me Down)" for Cher, who released it in 1966. The same year Nancy Sinatra recorded her darker version, Dalida sang it in Italian and Sheila in French, and the melody kept travelling from Yugoslavia and Hong Kong to Romania and the Czech Republic.
- [Strangers in the Night: the versions around the world](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/cover-atlas/strangers-in-the-night/): "Strangers in the Night" was composed by the German bandleader Bert Kaempfert and became a number one hit for Frank Sinatra in 1966. Within a few years it had German, French, Italian, Spanish, Japanese, Turkish and Russian versions.
- [Tombe la neige: the versions around the world](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/cover-atlas/tombe-la-neige/): "Tombe la neige" is a 1963 ballad by Salvatore Adamo, the Sicilian-born singer who grew up in Belgium. Adamo recorded it himself in Italian, German, Spanish and Japanese, and it was covered in Turkish by Ajda Pekkan and in Korean.
- [Those Were the Days: the Russian song behind the hit](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/cover-atlas/those-were-the-days/): "Those Were the Days" started as "Dorogoi dlinnoyu", a Russian romance from the 1920s made famous by Alexander Vertinsky. Gene Raskin wrote English lyrics, and Mary Hopkin's 1968 recording, produced by Paul McCartney, made it a worldwide hit with versions in French, Italian, German, Spanish, Turkish, Finnish and Polish.
- [Poupée de cire, poupée de son: the Eurovision winner in every language](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/cover-atlas/poupee-de-cire-poupee-de-son/): Serge Gainsbourg wrote "Poupée de cire, poupée de son" for France Gall, who won the 1965 Eurovision Song Contest with it for Luxembourg. Gall recorded it in German and Japanese herself, and it was covered in Czech, Danish, Finnish and Catalan.
- [Parole parole: the duet in every language](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/cover-atlas/parole-parole/): "Parole parole" was first recorded in 1972 by Mina with the actor Alberto Lupo. A year later Dalida and Alain Delon made it a hit in French as "Paroles, paroles", and the duet was recorded in Portuguese, German, Spanish, Japanese and Turkish.
- [Lambada isn't Brazilian. It's Bolivian.](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/cover-atlas/lambada/): The song the world knows as "Lambada" started as "Llorando se fue", recorded by the Bolivian group Los Kjarkas in 1981. It was covered in Peru and Brazil, became a worldwide hit for Kaoma in 1989, and was recorded in Arabic, Japanese, Korean, Turkish, Cantonese and Hindi.
- [Ya Mustafa: one Egyptian song, eight countries](https://bejofftherecord.com/series/cover-atlas/ya-mustafa/): "Ya Mustafa" is an Egyptian song. Bob Azzam's French version became a European hit in 1960, and the same year it was recorded in Spanish, Danish and Japanese, followed by German, Serbo-Croatian, Catalan and, in 1994, Hindi.
